newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW-Australian June labour force data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Australian June labour force data.

text.p: Australian employment rose by 11,900 in June following a fall of 40,300 in May, official figures showed. Full-time employment fell 16,900 in June.
The June unemployment rate was 8.5 percent, compared with 8.8 percent in May.

Forecasts for employment had centred on a 42,500 rise, and ranged from a rise of 25,000 to a rise of 60,000. For unemployment, forecasts had centred on a rate of 8.7 percent, and ranged from 8.6 to 8.9 percent.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follows.
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"These numbers are right at the bottom end of expectations, in fact they're lower than the lowest forecast which just shows how difficult it predict these volatile numbers. But they're very weak. There's no doubt that the trend in employment is very, very subdued at the moment. We think that the labour market is bottoming out, but I think this number will certainly increase the probability a little bit further, closer to 60-65 percent, that the Reserve Bank will cut rates in the next few weeks."
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HONG KONG BANK OF AUSTRALIA
"We think it's a very weak number, particularly the full-time employment fall of 16,900 following the fall in May. To our mind a rate cut is 70 percent likely on the 25th (of July), but not before."
BRUCE HOCKMAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"Certainly it's going to put the easing back at the forefront of their (the Reserve Bank) minds. I suppose the key question is did they have enough concern about this to have this as a contingency the last time they met. And also I wonder whether they may want to leave it a little while and actually try and get some consumer confidence effect by easing somewhat closer to the next consumer confidence survey."
BILL EVANS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"Obviously it was well below market expectations. To see a fall in full time employment was also disappointing. The fall in the unemployment rate is due to the fall in the participation rate, which is not a good sign for the economy. So it looks like it leaves the way open for another rate cut."
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA AUSTRALIA:

"The employment numbers are surprisingly weak. Certainly it is a real puzzle now as to why employment has been so weak so far this year. I would certainly have been looking for a bigger rebound for June. The employment numbers are well below where we'd normally expect to see them given the strength in both the Bureau of Statistics and the ANZ job vacancy series. My feeling is that in the next few months we should see some positive surprises on employment numbers. Certainly this keeps a rate cut firmly on the agenda. We'd be looking to a window of opportunity after the RBA August board meeting."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"A few people are getting a bit excited by the lower unemployment rate, but when you have got full time employment down again and total employment only just up 12,000 it doesn't sound like the labour market has got a lot of legs in it at the moment, it's pretty sick. Unfortunately, I'm not a member of the Reserve Bank board, but if I were I'd be advocating that they would have to ease up on monetary conditions and try to get the pace of the economy a little bit stronger so we can at least turn the labour market around."
GUY BRUTEN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, SBC WARBURG

"It looks like a fairly weak set of numbers to me. A rise of only 11,900 overall -- a lot weaker than the markets looking for and gives you a fairly weak picture over the last six months. I'm sort of unwilling to read to read too much into the full-time/part-time split, but full-time time employment has been pretty soft over most of this year, a lot softer than part-time. We were on the easing side of things anyway, so that just keeps us there. I think the key bit of information is really CPI and wages (later this month)."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"Full time employment is still extremely weak and has fallen something like 40,000 in the past two months and its lowest point in about 18 months. The participation rate fall to 63.0 is the lowest in three years, so that suggests to me a mounting discouraged worker effect and that's the only reason why the unemployment rate came back. It is a very, very weak result. Total employment for the first half of this year is fractionally lower than where it was at the end of December. Given that we have got inflation data coming up in a couple of weeks and that looks very, very benign, the issue is when are they (the RBA) going to ease, and I think that you keep watching the screens."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
